programme: CREBBP (CBP) acting as the histone-acetyltransferase coactivator for NFIA-directed differentiation transcription: NFIA binds its target loci and recruits CBP to acetylate chromatin and drive transcriptional output; when CBP's coactivator function is lost or diverted, NFIA-dependent differentiation programmes fail to execute.
role_in_a: In Huntington's Disease, CBP/CREBBP coactivator function is the factor most directly documented here: it is implicated as a shared hub in polyglutamine-disease protein-complex and bioinformatic analyses (PMID 37298574, 36902304), and NFIA itself is directly shown to mark a failure of astrocyte maturation in HD iPSC and mouse models (PMID 36590162) — consistent with a CBP-dependent differentiation programme going unexecuted in HD glia.
role_in_b: In papillary kidney carcinoma, CREBBP appears among the genes profiled in a renal-cell-carcinoma genomic cohort (PMID 37427096), and NFIA is reported to carry prognostic significance across human cancers including papillary renal cell carcinoma (PMID 32219034) — consistent with loss of an NFIA/CBP-driven tubular-epithelial differentiation programme accompanying tumour progression.
shared_axis: Both diseases can be framed as a failure of the same coactivator-dependent differentiation circuit — CBP-supported NFIA transcription maintaining astrocyte identity in the brain and tubular epithelial identity in the kidney — so that when CBP's acetyltransferase output is compromised (by mutant huntingtin sequestration in HD, by genomic/epigenomic disruption in the tumour), the NFIA programme in each tissue collapses toward an immature or dedifferentiated state. This specific cross-disease link is inference from parallel, independent findings, not a stated connection in the retrieved literature.
reasoning: Each carrying factor is independently placed in both diseases by retrieved papers, so the module is more than a coincidence of counts, but the papers themselves are hedged (reader's notes flag 'may be relevant', 'limited detail', bioinformatics/genomic-profiling rather than mechanistic studies), and CREBBP+NFIA is a thin, two-node module rather than a well-characterized named complex. The other ten concordant factors (ARID4A/SIN3A-HDAC repression, ZNF202/KAP1-HP1 repression, HEY2 and KLF9 as Notch/corepressor-associated repressors, circadian HLF/RORB, AP-1 FOSL1, MLX/glucose-sensing, LRRFIP1, FOXD2) pull in unrelated or opposing chromatin directions and do not join this or any other single story, so they are excluded rather than forced in.
support: PMID 36590162 — direct HD evidence: NFIA implicated in impaired astrocyte maturation in HD iPSC/mouse transcriptomes. PMID 32219034 — direct PRCC evidence: NFI family (including NFIA) has prognostic significance in human cancers, reported to include papillary renal cell carcinoma. PMID 37298574 — HD-adjacent: CREBBP appears in a polyglutamine-disease protein-complex/splicing-modulator study. PMID 36902304 — HD-adjacent: CREBBP flagged as a shared hub gene in an integrated bioinformatics analysis referencing HD. PMID 37427096 — PRCC-adjacent, uncertain: CREBBP mentioned in a small Chinese renal-cell-carcinoma genomic-profiling cohort, relevance to the papillary subtype not confirmed from the text shown.
how_to_falsify: In HD patient-derived (or mouse) astrocytes, test by co-immunoprecipitation whether CREBBP/CBP physically associates with NFIA at chromatin, and whether CBP HAT-activity inhibition (or expression of mutant huntingtin) blocks induction of NFIA target genes tied to astrocyte maturation; in parallel, in papillary RCC cell lines, test whether CREBBP knockdown phenocopies NFIA loss on tubular-differentiation marker expression. If NFIA target activation is unaffected by CREBBP loss in either system, the proposed coactivator dependency — and thus the shared axis — is wrong.
caveats: Only 2 independent cohort pairs underlie the 294 reported patient-group comparisons, so recurrence counts (100+/294 for most factors) reflect repeated slicing of the same two cohorts by clinical variable, not 294 independent replications — treat the concordance fractions as considerably weaker than they look. The tissue pairing is blood (HD) vs kidney (PRCC), so a blood-derived HD network may not reflect CNS-specific CBP/NFIA biology directly. Literature coverage is thin overall (many factors returned nothing), and the single-view exclusions (RARA, MED1, MED23 — other nuclear-receptor/Mediator coactivator-adjacent factors) show that a broader 'general coactivator' story did not survive across patient groups, which is why this account is deliberately narrowed to CREBBP and NFIA rather than a larger coactivator module. Tissue-generic exclusions (STAT1/STAT2/IRF7/IRF8, EZH2, ETS1, MEF2C, RORA, KLF2, CREB5, HLX, LMO2) confirm the concordant signal is not simply generic blood/immune or Polycomb-repression activity.
